source: Klein, Moon, Hoffman (2006) Making sense of sensemaking 2: a macrocognitive model, IEEE Intelligent Systems 21(5):88-92
finding: Founding statement of the data-frame model. Sensemaking is a two-way fit: data are fitted into a frame and a frame is fitted around the data. Neither comes first. Full text could not be opened (IEEE and mirrors blocked); only the Crossref record and its reference list were read.
numbers: Crossref: cited by 394 works. Part 1 (Alternative perspectives, IEEE Intell Syst 21(4):70-73) cited by 576. Reference list has 22 items.
limits: Primary text not read. All content of the founding theory below comes from secondary papers that were opened.
agent_relevance: S2 should hold a current frame and the data together and let each reshape the other, not run data then explanation in one pass.

source: Gary Klein site, Data-Frame Theory page
finding: Klein states the theory arose in 2006 with Moon and Hoffman. Data are signals of events. Frames are explanatory structures that account for the data and guide the search for more data.
numbers: No numbers on the page.
quote: sensemaking is the process of fitting data into a frame and fitting a frame around the data
limits: Short overview with no activities list or cases.
agent_relevance: Gives the shortest usable spec of S2: a frame plus a data set, with a search driven by the frame.

source: Reference list of Klein, Moon, Hoffman 2006b (via Crossref)
finding: The macrocognitive paper builds on Feltovich 1997 (expert flexibility), Klein 1995 (mental simulation), Heuer 1999 (Psychology of Intelligence Analysis), Rudolph 2003 (Into the Big Muddy), Sieck (questioning strategies for a surprise), Cohen 2003 (critical thinking dialogue), Dreyfus 1979, Gentner 1983 (mental models), Klein 1998 (Sources of Power). It also cites Klein 2006 'A Data/Frame Theory of Sensemaking'.
numbers: 22 references. 9 resolved to author and title, the rest had no metadata.
limits: Reference list only; says what was cited, not how.
agent_relevance: Backward links to follow: fixation and surprise (Rudolph, Sieck), expert flexibility (Feltovich), analyst mind-sets (Heuer).

source: Pontis & Blandford (2015/2016) Understanding 'influence': an empirical test of the data-frame theory of sensemaking, JASIST
finding: Most direct empirical test found. 11 UCL researchers (6 with HCI expertise, 5 novices) did four 'influence' tasks, two in a familiar field (HCI) and two in an unfamiliar one (chemistry), with think-aloud and interviews. The D/F model fitted most activities, but 'seeking and inferring new relationships', 'tracking anomalies' and 'seeking a new frame' did not appear.
numbers: N=11 participants, 4 tasks each, 44 task runs. Participants combined 2 to 12 influence indicators per task, 4 or 5 indicator types each.
limits: Small qualitative sample, structure tasks not narrative tasks, one domain (academia). Authors say the theory is dominant but 'has not been extensively tested'.
agent_relevance: Reframing and anomaly tracking may not happen on their own in a task with no narrative. An agent should force an explicit anomaly log; people did not do it.

source: Pontis & Blandford (2015) same study: one frame only
finding: In all 44 task runs participants worked with only one frame. They did not track two or three rival frames, unlike narrative sensemaking in Klein 2007. The authors call candidate people 'frame instantiations' instead.
numbers: 44 of 44 task runs used a single frame. Klein 2007 is quoted as saying people track up to three alternative frames at once.
limits: Structure tasks (who is influential) differ from story tasks. May be a task boundary, not a refutation.
agent_relevance: Comparing frames is not natural even for humans; the schema must force it, not assume it.

source: Pontis & Blandford (2015) frame-recognition order
finding: The theory says frame and data search occur together (chicken and egg). In this study participants first recognised the problem and built a frame, then searched for data. A frame was needed to start a productive search.
numbers: First action in the mapped sensemaking chains (Figs 6, 7) was recognising the problem, then building the frame, in all analysed cases (E2, E3, N4, N6).
limits: Qualitative coding on four of 11 participants in detail.
agent_relevance: Supports a first step of 'state a frame, then collect data' rather than blind data gathering.

source: Pontis & Blandford (2015) novice vs expert paths
finding: Experts leaned on prior knowledge as soft evidence and elaborated the frame more; novices needed hard evidence and took shorter, simpler journeys. Experts also questioned source credibility more often.
numbers: Example task 3: novice N6 had 6 data points; expert E2 had 15 data points and discarded more.
limits: Two exemplar participants, not group statistics. No effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Expert behaviour is more elaboration plus source checks. A scaffold can copy this: fill the frame slots, then check the source of each datum.

source: Klein et al. (2007) seven data-frame activities, as listed by Pontis & Blandford
finding: Seven activities (Klein et al. 2007, pp 132-142): mapping data and frame; elaborating a frame; questioning a frame; preserving a frame; comparing frames; reframing; seeking a frame. Elaboration continues until anomalies show the frame must be replaced. Questioning starts at inconsistency, before certainty that the frame is wrong. Preserving means inconsistencies judged not strong enough to drop the frame.
numbers: Seven activities. Maximum of three alternative frames at once, reported by Pontis & Blandford as Klein's claim, with no explanation given.
limits: Second-hand description. Primary chapter not opened.
agent_relevance: Maps directly to S2 operators and O8 reframe: elaborate, question on inconsistency, preserve with a reason, compare, reframe, seek.

source: Klein et al. (2007) anchors and conceptual strain, as reported by Pontis & Blandford
finding: Data used as anchors for one frame should not be reused as anchors for a second frame, to avoid conceptual strain. Participants kept one frame because they recombined the same anchors across tasks.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Second-hand; mechanism of anchors not tested.
agent_relevance: When reframing, a new frame should not lean on the same anchor facts as the old one, or the reframe is cosmetic.

source: Sieck, Klein, Peluso et al. (2007) FOCUS: a model of sensemaking (ARI report ADA469770)
finding: Army report extending the data-frame model with a list of activities (elaborate, question, preserve, compare, seek a frame; one listing differs on the sixth item). Applied to Bosnia peacekeeping scenarios and navigation problems per Pontis & Blandford. Full text blocked (403 and HTML shell), not opened.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened. Known only via a search summary and Pontis & Blandford.
agent_relevance: Worth a retry for exact trial counts on frame questioning in exercises.

source: Prochaska, Vera, Tan et al. (2024) Misleading Ourselves: how disinformation manipulates sensemaking (arXiv 2410.14858)
finding: Applies data-frame theory to election rumours. A false frame (rigged election) dictates which data are noticed. 'Frame fixation' is defined as being stuck on a single explanation. Amateurs lack the frame repertoire of experts, who narrow to plausible explanations.
numbers: About 1000 coded tweets: 5 rumours, 100 coded tweets each per election year, 2020 and 2022, 500 per year.
limits: Qualitative case study of social media, not a test of the theory's predictions. Notes the models 'do not fully account for an adversarial environment'.
agent_relevance: A frame supplied by the prompt (or by an adversarial context) steers which data an LLM attends to; the S2 frame must be produced by the agent, not accepted from the input.

source: Klein et al. (2007) frame fixation and expertise, as reported by Prochaska et al.
finding: Klein et al. said expertise comes from a larger number and better quality of frames. Experts do better partly because they narrow sensemaking to likely plausible explanations. The same narrowing is a weakness when disinformation targets plausibility.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Plausibility-driven narrowing is a feature and a risk; a check that tests the frame on held-out data (G3) guards the risk.

source: Heuer (1999) Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, ch. 2 on mind-sets (CIA)
finding: Mind-sets form fast and resist change. Data are assimilated into existing images, more so when information is ambiguous. Heuer's account of Bruner and Potter (1964): those who started viewing a picture most out of focus needed a clearer picture to name it than those who started less blurred. Longer exposure to blur also raised the clarity needed.
numbers: Bruner & Potter 1964, Science 144:424-25. Heuer gives no sample size or percentages. Ordering of effects only.
quote: the initial interpretation is maintained until the contradiction becomes so obvious
limits: Heuer summarises; the numbers are not in his text. Perception task, not a field study.
agent_relevance: Early wrong frames cost more evidence to dislodge than was needed to form them. Do not commit to a frame from the first ambiguous cues; keep it tentative.

source: Heuer (1999): information needed to overturn a hypothesis
finding: The early but wrong impression persists because the evidence needed to invalidate a hypothesis is considerably greater than the evidence needed to make the first interpretation. Shifting perspective is hard; Heuer uses the old woman/young woman figure to show it.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Argument by analogy from perception experiments.
agent_relevance: Supports a rule that O8 reframe needs a threshold of inconsistent evidence that the code counts, not a feeling.

source: Wikipedia, Sensemaking (information science), data-frame section
finding: Describes sensemaking as two-way. Data evoke frames and frames select and connect data. When fit is poor, data may be reconsidered or the frame revised. Lists KMH 2006a and 2006b as the references.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Tertiary; the page gives its own account.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Zheng, Miller, Bialkowski, Soyer, Janda (2025) Supporting data-frame dynamics in AI-assisted decision making (arXiv 2504.15894)
finding: First compact formal model of the data-frame loop found. Raw information gives evidence E_t by an extraction function. A retrieval function picks a hypothesis set H_t. A scoring function s(E,h) in [0,1] scores each. If the best score is below a threshold tau, the next step extracts more evidence, retrieves more hypotheses, or both. Stop when some hypothesis has s >= tau.
numbers: Formula: h* = argmax over H_T of s(E_T,h), subject to s >= tau. Prototype: concept bottleneck model on derm7pt with 7 dermoscopy concepts. No user study yet.
limits: Position paper with a prototype; no measured results. Maps data to evidence and frame to hypothesis, a narrowing of Klein's frame concept.
agent_relevance: A ready spec for S2 as code: extract, retrieve, score, threshold, loop. Code, not the model, holds tau and the stop test (G5).

source: Zheng et al. (2025) on anchoring and fixation in AI support
finding: Typical AI decision support fixes on a single data-frame structure (one recommendation) and so misses alternatives. Human decision makers may quickly anchor on a few pieces of evidence (key anchoring data per Klein). When human and AI hypotheses differ, the relation turns from collaboration to competition, with risk of overreliance.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Claims are argued, not measured, in this paper.
agent_relevance: An agent should output a hypothesis set with evidence for and against each, not one answer.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR; arXiv 2310.01798), oracle labels
finding: With oracle labels telling the model when the answer is wrong, self-correction (a reframe) helps. GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, CSQA 82.0 to 85.5, HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0 (row pairing read from garbled table text).
numbers: Test sets: 100 for HotpotQA; others larger (exact N not read). Max two correction rounds.
limits: The oracle makes the gain uninformative about true self-correction. Table pairings inferred from text extraction.
agent_relevance: Reframing works when a real signal says the frame failed (G2). Matches 'revise only from real output'.

source: Huang et al. (2024) intrinsic self-correction without oracle
finding: Without external feedback, asking the model to rethink lowers accuracy. GPT-3.5 CSQA fell from 75.8 to 38.1 (round 1) and 41.8 (round 2). GPT-4 GSM8K fell from 95.5 to 91.5 and 89.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 49.0 then 43.0. Llama-2 GSM8K fell from 62.0 to 43.5 then 36.5.
numbers: GPT-3.5 kept its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time; when it changed, correct-to-wrong was more common than wrong-to-correct. GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 to 88.0 to 90.0.
limits: Prompted self-review is a poor stand-in for a human noticing a mismatch. Different prompts (Table 5) did not help.
agent_relevance: Questioning a frame by asking the model to doubt itself is unsafe. Trigger doubt from counted evidence only (G1).

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs get lost in multi-turn conversation (arXiv 2505.06120)
finding: Frame fixation shows in LLMs. Across 15 LLMs, 200,000+ simulated conversations and six tasks, performance fell 39% on average from fully specified single-turn to underspecified multi-turn input. Aptitude (best case) fell about 15% but unreliability (best minus worst case) rose 112%. Models make early assumptions, propose answers too early and rely on their own earlier wrong attempts.
numbers: Average performance fell from about 90% to 60% (paper text). Aptitude -15%, unreliability +112%.
quote: when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover
limits: Synthetic sharded tasks and simulated users; six generation tasks only.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue of data/frame fixation. A wrong early frame persists, so restart from the raw data rather than extending the agent's own transcript.

source: Choube et al. (2025) GLOSS: group of LLMs for open-ended sensemaking of passive sensing data (arXiv 2507.05461)
finding: Multi-LLM system modelled on Klein et al. and Pirolli & Card: an information-seeking and elaboration loop and a sensemaking and reframing loop. On objective queries it got 87.93% accuracy and 66.19% consistency against 29.31% and 52.85% for a plain RAG baseline.
numbers: 60 objective queries for accuracy (paired t(59)=8.24, p<.001), 210 for consistency (t(59)=3.33, p=.001). 244 queries in all: 196 objective, 34 subjective, 14 mixed.
limits: Gain mostly from generating code to compute answers, as the authors state; the frame loop is not ablated alone. Single domain (passive sensing).
agent_relevance: A two-loop design works in practice, but the evidence points to code execution as the active ingredient, in line with G5.

source: Li et al. (2025) Vital Insight: expert sensemaking of tracking data with human-in-the-loop LLM (arXiv 2410.14879)
finding: LLM-generated daily summaries had 91.49% correct facts (215 of 235), 2.13% wrong, against expert-written summaries at 83.82% correct (114 of 136) and 11.03% wrong. Experts with the AI took about 14.7 seconds longer per task and rated satisfaction higher. No significant difference in answer correctness.
numbers: SUS usability: with LLM mean 73.42 (SD 17.92), without 70.53 (SD 19.59); Wilcoxon p<.05, effect size 0.44. Similarity of same-day LLM summaries 0.52 (SD 0.15) vs experts 0.23 (SD 0.11).
limits: Fact check done by the first author alone. The data-frame model is cited only in related work.
agent_relevance: LLM fact-level accuracy on summaries is high; the gap is in interpretation (frame), not in reading data.

source: Huang, Fatir, Luo et al. (2025) Narrative Scaffolding (arXiv 2512.18920)
finding: Tool that operationalises the data-frame idea as 'investigation', testing interpretive frames against evidence. Formative survey of 48 analysts: 44 of 48 left reasoning undocumented, 32 of 48 rarely reviewed past conclusions, 33 of 48 had trouble weighing rival explanations, 29 of 48 restarted when reasoning failed.
numbers: Within-subject study N=20: time per insight 2.31 min (SD 0.76) with the tool vs 4.62 min (SD 1.22) baseline, p<0.001. System check N=6.
limits: Self-report survey; gains are speed and insight count, not correct frames. Authors say bias reduction is not shown.
agent_relevance: Writing the working frame down as an artefact and revisiting it is the mechanism; an agent can keep a frame log the code reads.

source: Bamman et al. (2024) On classification with LLMs in cultural analytics (arXiv 2410.12029); negative search note
finding: Paper read and does not use Klein's data-frame model. Recorded as a negative search result: no LLM study found that tests data-frame predictions (anchoring, reframing, frame count) directly.
numbers: Search budget used: 4 web searches, plus failed Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv API queries (rate limited); zero hits for a direct LLM test.
limits: Absence of evidence in a limited search, not proof.
agent_relevance: Our schema's S2 would be among the first direct tests; no external benchmark to lean on.

source: Pirolli & Card (2005) and Russell et al. (1993) rival models, via Pontis & Blandford
finding: Russell et al. 1993 treat sensemaking as modelling with schemas; Pirolli and Card 2005 give an information-foraging loop and a sensemaking loop for intelligence analysis. Klein differs by the two-way data-frame link and the explicit frame-questioning activities.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Second-hand; Pirolli & Card PDF could not be fetched.
agent_relevance: GLOSS borrows both. Klein's version supplies the doubt and reframe operators we want.

source: Weick (1995) Sensemaking in Organizations, via Prochaska et al.
finding: Weick: sensemaking is driven by plausibility over accuracy, grounded in identity, and social. Klein's theory is described as an extension of Weick's. A good story holds elements together 'long enough to energize and guide action'.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Second-hand quotation.
agent_relevance: A frame is good enough to act if plausible; our G3 adds a held-out check so plausible is not enough.

source: Klein, Phillips, Rall, Peluso (2007) A data-frame theory of sensemaking, in Expertise out of context (NDM6), pp 113-155
finding: The founding chapter. Full text not obtainable (ResearchGate 403, PsycNet blocked). Known only from opened secondary papers: seven activities, anchors, frame fixation, max three frames, experts hold more and better frames.
numbers: None verified from the primary.
limits: Not opened. Case sample sizes in the chapter are unknown to me.
agent_relevance: Highest-value item to retrieve in a later pass.
